samples.text:
In many countries today, children begin formal education at a younger age than before, sometimes when they are only three or four years old. I believe this is mostly a positive development for children and also for their parents.

Firstly, starting school early helps children to learn basic skills. At a young age, children's brains develop very quickly, so they can learn letters, numbers and even a foreign language more easily than older children. If they start school early, they will be more prepared when they go to primary school, and they can do better in their studies later.

Secondly, school gives young children the chance to make friends and learn how to behave with other people. At home, a child may only play with their parents or one brother or sister. At school, they must share toys, wait their turn and follow the rules of teacher. These social skills are very important for their future life. Also, early education is helpful for parents. Today, in many families both mother and father work full-time, so they need a safe place for their children during the day. When children go to school, parents can work without worry, and the family have more income.

However, some people think that young children need more time to play and they may feel stress if they study too much. This is true, so schools for small children should focus on games and activities, not on exams.

In conclusion, I think that children starting formal education earlier is a positive development, because it helps their learning and social skills, and it also support working parents.

samples.text:
In many parts of the world, children are now expected to begin formal schooling, with structured lessons in reading, writing and mathematics, at an increasingly early age. Although this is usually intended to give children a head start, I believe it is largely a negative development.

Supporters of early education argue that young children learn quickly and that starting sooner will lead to higher achievement later. It also meets the needs of working parents, who require reliable childcare, and can help children from disadvantaged backgrounds who may receive little educational support at home.

However, many young children are simply not ready for formal learning. At the age of three or four, most children learn best through play, exploration and conversation rather than by sitting at desks completing worksheets. When they are pushed to read and write before they are developmentally ready, some become frustrated and may begin to see learning as something difficult and unpleasant. This negative attitude can last for years and affect their motivation throughout school.

In addition, an early focus on academic skills can leave less time for developing other important abilities. Through unstructured play, children learn to solve problems, cooperate with others, manage their emotions and use their imagination. These qualities are essential for success in later life, yet they cannot be easily measured in tests, so they are often given lower priority in formal classrooms. Furthermore, children who spend long days in a structured environment from such a young age may experience stress and tiredness, which affect their wellbeing.

In conclusion, while early education can provide childcare and support for some families, introducing formal lessons too early may harm children's attitude to learning and limit their broader development. I therefore regard this trend as mainly negative, and I believe the early years should focus on play-based learning.
samples.why: Clear negative position throughout · opposing view summarised then main ideas well extended · logical organisation · good vocabulary (head start, developmentally ready) · largely error-free with a minor slip.

samples.text:
Across many countries, the age at which children first enter a classroom and begin structured academic instruction has steadily fallen. This is generally justified as an investment in children's future achievement, but I would argue that, in most cases, it is a negative development.

The rationale for early schooling is not without merit. High-quality early education can narrow the gap between children from affluent and disadvantaged homes, since the latter may have fewer books and less adult conversation at home. For families in which both parents work, early school entry also provides dependable, affordable care.

Yet there is a crucial distinction between early education and early formal education. What benefits young children most is a rich environment of play, talk and exploration, in which language, curiosity and social skills develop naturally. Formal instruction, by contrast, demands sustained attention, fine motor control and the ability to sit still, capacities that many four-year-olds have not yet acquired. Children pushed into reading and arithmetic before they are ready may struggle, and early experiences of failure can shape a lasting belief that they are not good at learning.

There is also a question of opportunity cost. Every hour spent on phonics drills or worksheets is an hour not spent building with blocks, negotiating games with peers or inventing stories, activities through which children develop the creativity, resilience and self-regulation that underpin later success. Several countries with consistently strong educational outcomes do not begin formal schooling until around the age of six or seven, which suggests that an early start is by no means a prerequisite for high achievement.

In conclusion, while providing young children with stimulating care is highly desirable, subjecting them to formal academic instruction at an ever earlier age risks undermining both their wellbeing and their long-term enthusiasm for learning. This trend is therefore, on balance, a regrettable one.
samples.why: Clear negative judgement built on a precise distinction · ideas fully extended and logically sequenced · concession handled deftly · wide, accurate vocabulary (opportunity cost, self-regulation) · complex structures with full control.
